title: States, actions and rewards
objectives: Model a problem as a Markov decision process and write the discounted return.

screens.title: A dice game with no last roll
screens.prose: Roll a die and take its pips in pounds, or reroll. There is no limit on rerolls, but each costs time: a prize taken one roll later is worth 0.9 of the same prize now. Try the rule "keep a 5 or a 6, otherwise reroll".
screens.question: Call the game's value under this rule $V$. Then a reroll is worth $0.9V$. What is $V$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Condition on the first roll, as in `markov` first-step analysis.
With chance $\tfrac26$ you keep 5 or 6, worth 5.5 on average; with chance $\tfrac46$ you get $0.9V$.
$V = \tfrac{5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac46 \times 0.9V$, so $0.4V = \tfrac{11}{6}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write one equation for $V$ by conditioning on the first roll.

byKey.no-discount: That is the average of 5 and 6. A reroll is not free: it is worth $0.9V$, and you reroll two times in three.
byKey.mean: That is one roll with no choice. Rerolling the low rolls is worth more.
byKey.keep-only: That is $\tfrac{11}{6}$, the kept part alone. Add the $\tfrac46 \times 0.9V$ from rerolling.

explain.text: Keeping 5 or 6 gives $\tfrac{11}{6}$; the other four rolls give $0.9V$. So $V = \tfrac{11}{6} + 0.6V$ and $V = \tfrac{55}{12} = 4.5833$. There is no last roll to work back from: $V$ appears on both sides.

screens.title: Which rule is best?
screens.prose: A rule keeps any roll of at least $k$. Its value is $V_k = \dfrac{\tfrac16(k + \dots + 6)}{1 - \gamma\,\tfrac{k - 1}{6}}$, by the same first-step equation. The bars show $V_k$. Move $\gamma$, the factor a reroll keeps.

params.xLabel: Keep any roll of at least

screens.question: At $\gamma = 0.9$, which threshold gives the most valuable rule?

options.why: At 0.9 waiting for a 6 costs too much: that rule is worth £4.00.
Close, at £4.55, but keeping 4s gives up a little.
Never rerolling is worth only £3.50, the plain mean.

feedback.correct: Keeping 5 or 6 is worth £4.58, the most of the six rules.
feedback.generic: Set $\gamma$ to 0.9 and read the tallest bar.

explain.text: At $\gamma = 0.9$ the values are 3.50, 3.92, 4.29, 4.55, 4.58 and 4.00. Keep 5 or 6: a 4 is worth less than rerolling, $0.9 \times 4.5833 = 4.125$. As $\gamma$ nears 1, waiting for a 6 wins.

screens.title: A Markov decision process
screens.prose: That game is a **Markov decision process**: a **state** $s$, an **action** $a$, a **transition** chance $p(s' \mid s, a)$, a **reward** $r$ and a **discount** $\gamma$. A **policy** picks an action in each state. The course gridworld is one too: move U, R, D or L; +1 and −1 end the episode; each move costs 0.04.

state.caption: Start at row 4, column 1. The wall cannot be entered.

screens.question: How many cells of the gridworld are states where the agent must still choose an action?

hints.text: Count the 20 cells, then take away those where no choice is made.
The wall is not a state; the two end cells need no action.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave out the wall and the two end cells.

byKey.all: You counted every cell, including the wall the agent can never stand in.
byKey.with-terms: The +1 and −1 cells end the episode, so no action is chosen there.
byKey.no-wall-only: Leave out both end cells, not one.

explain.text: Twenty cells less the wall leaves 19 states, and two of them end the episode. So 17 states call for an action. The **Markov property** holds: where the agent goes next depends only on the cell and the action, not on how it got there.

screens.title: A slippery floor
screens.prose: On the **slippery** grid the intended move happens with chance 0.8; with chance 0.1 each the agent slips to one side instead. A move into the wall or off the grid leaves it where it is. The agent stands at row 3, column 1 and chooses U.
screens.question: Shade every cell the agent can be in after this move.

hints.text: The three possible moves are U, and the side moves L and R.
L from column 1 runs off the grid.
U reaches row 2, R reaches column 2, and L stays put.

feedback.correct: Up with 0.8, right with 0.1, and a slip left bumps the edge: stay with 0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow each of the three moves, including the slips.

byKey.no-stay: You missed the slip to the left. It hits the edge, so the agent stays in its cell.
byKey.only-up: The floor is slippery: one move in five goes sideways.

explain.text: $p(\text{r2c1}) = 0.8$, $p(\text{r3c2}) = 0.1$ and $p(\text{r3c1}) = 0.1$. A slip into the edge counts as staying. The chances depend only on the cell and the action.

screens.title: The return of one path
screens.prose: The **return** from time $t$ is $G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \dots$ On the **deterministic** grid (no slips) the agent goes from row 1, column 2 right three times to the +1. Each move pays −0.04, and entering +1 pays $1 - 0.04 = 0.96$.
screens.question: What is the return of this path, with $\gamma = 0.9$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Three rewards: −0.04, −0.04, then 0.96.
Discount the second by 0.9 and the third by $0.9^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight the rewards 1, 0.9 and 0.81 in order.

byKey.no-discount: You added the rewards without discounting. The later ones count for less.
byKey.no-step: You left out the step costs. Every move pays −0.04, the last one included.
byKey.disc-first: You discounted the first reward too. It arrives after one step and counts in full.

explain.text: $G = -0.04 + 0.9(-0.04) + 0.9^2(0.96) = 0.7016$. Three moves from the goal is the best this cell can do, so 0.7016 will reappear as its value.

screens.title: The discount as patience
screens.prose: A reward $k$ steps away counts $\gamma^k$ of its face value now. That is how a desk discounts cash: with interest rate $i$ per step, £1 in $k$ steps is worth $1/(1 + i)^k$ today, so $\gamma = 1/(1 + i)$.
screens.question: With $\gamma = 0.9$, what is £1 received 10 steps from now worth today? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Each step multiplies by 0.9.
Ten steps multiply by $0.9^{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by 0.9 once for each of the 10 steps.

byKey.linear: You took 10% off ten times from the original pound. Each step takes 10% of what is left.
byKey.nine: That is nine steps. Count ten.

explain.text: £1 in 10 steps is worth $0.9^{10} = 0.3487$ now. A $\gamma$ of 0.9 is impatient, like an interest rate of $1/0.9 - 1 = 11\%$ a step; 0.99 is patient.

screens.title: A bump on the way
screens.prose: On the deterministic grid the agent at row 2, column 4 first moves L into the wall, which leaves it where it is. It then moves U, then R into the +1.
screens.question: What is the return of these three moves, with $\gamma = 0.9$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Three rewards: −0.04 for the bump, −0.04 for U, then 0.96.
The bump is a move like the others: it pays 0.04 and the next reward is discounted once more.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count three rewards, with 1, 0.9 and $0.9^2$ as their weights.

byKey.no-bump: You skipped the bump. The agent stays put, but the move still costs 0.04 and uses up a step of the discount.
byKey.free-bump: You gave the bump no reward. Every move pays the step cost, even one that goes nowhere.
byKey.no-step: You left out the step costs: each of the three moves pays −0.04 and the +1 pays $1 - 0.04$.

explain.text: $G = -0.04 + 0.9 \times (-0.04) + 0.81 \times 0.96 = 0.7016$. A bump into a wall changes nothing but the clock: it pays the step cost and delays every later reward.

screens.title: Code the pieces
screens.prose: Write `discounted_return(rewards, gamma)`. Then `transition(s, a, slip)`: the intended move with chance `1 - 2*slip` and each side move in `SIDES[a]` with `slip`, adding chances that land in the same cell. Then `dice_value(gamma, tol)`, iterating the game's equation from 0.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests. Values are compared with `math.isclose`; transition dicts must have the same cells with the same chances.

mutants.symptom: out[t] = p, so a corner loses chance.

hints.text: `move` already handles the wall and the edges.
In `transition`, two moves can land in the same cell: add their chances.
`dice_value` repeats `new = sum(max(x, gamma * V) for x in range(1, 7)) / 6`.

feedback.correct: All pass. In the corner, a blocked move and a slip both leave the agent in place: 0.9 in all.
feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Check the corner case, where two moves stay put, and the stopping rule in `dice_value`.

explain.text: `transition` builds the model $p(s' \mid s, a)$ that later lessons sum over. `dice_value` finds the game's value by repeating its own equation, a fixed point; lesson 7 does the same for the grid.

screens.title: Rewards for ever
screens.prose: A quoting rule earns £1 every step for ever, with no end state.
screens.question: With $\gamma = 0.9$, what is the return $\sum_{k \ge 0} 0.9^k \times 1$?

hints.text: It is a geometric series.
The sum of $\gamma^k$ from $k = 0$ is $\tfrac{1}{1 - \gamma}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Sum the geometric series $1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + \dots$

byKey.disc-first: You discounted the first pound too. The series starts at $\gamma^0 = 1$.
byKey.gamma: That is the second term only.
byKey.inverse: That is $1 - \gamma$. The sum is its reciprocal.

explain.text: $1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + \dots = \tfrac{1}{1 - 0.9} = 10$. With $\gamma = 1$ and no end state the sum grows without limit, so values are infinite and policies cannot be compared. A discount below 1, or an end the agent reaches, keeps them finite.

screens.title: The pieces of an MDP
screens.prose: An MDP is states, actions, transitions $p(s' \mid s, a)$, rewards and a discount $\gamma$. A policy $\pi$ chooses $a = \pi(s)$. The return $$G_t = \sum_{k \ge 0} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}$$ counts the first reward in full. Markov means the next state depends on the current state and action only.
screens.question: Which of these breaks the Markov property for the gridworld?

options.text: Slips are more likely right after a slip

options.why: A larger slip chance is still decided by the cell and the action alone.
A step cost is a reward. It still depends only on the move made.
The discount weights rewards. It does not change what the next cell depends on.

feedback.correct: If the last move matters, the cell alone no longer tells you the chances.
feedback.generic: Ask what the next cell would depend on in each case.

explain.text: Making slips depend on the previous move means the state must also remember that move. Add it to the state and the process is Markov again.

screens.title: Selling against a deadline
screens.prose: A desk must sell 4 lots within 5 steps. Each step it sells 0, 1 or 2 lots; selling more at once moves the price further, and the impact fades by the next step. Unsold lots at the end are dumped at a poor price.
screens.question: Which state makes this an MDP?

hints.text: Ask what the best sale this step depends on.
It depends on how much is left to sell and how long remains.
Impact fades, so past sales matter only through the lots left.

options.why: With 3 lots left, one step to go and four steps to go call for different sales. Steps left must be in the state.
The best sale depends on how much is still to sell. Lots left must be in the state.

options.text: The whole history of past sales
options.why: That works, but it is more than needed: past sales matter only through the lots left, since impact fades.

feedback.correct: Lots left and steps left: together they fix what is possible and what comes next.
feedback.generic: Ask what the best sale this step depends on.

explain.text: Lots left and steps left give 5 × 6 = 30 states, and the next state depends only on them and the lots sold. If impact lingered, the last sale would have to join the state.

ideas: A Markov decision process has states, actions, transition chances $p(s' \mid s, a)$, rewards and a discount $\gamma$; a policy picks an action per state.
The return $G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}$ counts the first reward in full and later ones less. With $\gamma < 1$ a stream of bounded rewards has a finite return.
With no last roll, a value satisfies its own equation, $V = E[\max(X, \gamma V)]$ in the dice game, and is found as a fixed point rather than by working back.

formula.name: Discounted return
formula.note: Finite for bounded rewards when $\gamma < 1$, or when every path reaches an end state.

summary.trap: Forgetting the step cost, or discounting the first reward. Both shift every value in the grid.

quiz.question: What is the chance it stays where it is? Give a decimal to 1 place.

byKey.slip: The intended move L also runs off the grid.

quiz.prose: In the unlimited dice game with $\gamma = 0.9$, the game is worth £4.58.
quiz.question: You roll a 4. What should you do?

options.text: Reroll: a reroll is worth $0.9 \times 4.5833 \approx 4.125$, more than 4
Keep it: 4 is above the average roll of 3.5
options.why: The comparison is with what rerolling is worth, $0.9 \times 4.5833 \approx 4.125$, not with one roll.

options.text: Either: a 4 is worth about the same as the game
options.why: Rerolling is worth 4.125, which beats 4 by 12.5p.

options.text: Keep it, because waiting is discounted
options.why: The discount is already in the 4.125. Even after it, rerolling wins.

explain.text: Stop when the roll beats the value of going on, $0.9 \times 4.5833 = 4.125$. So keep only 5 or 6.
